          Five Knee-Jerk Reactions to Premier League 2026-27 Matchday 8
        
      
                          
                      Oct 26, 2026
          
                      Ali Tweedale / Author
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
We round up the weekend’s Premier League action by jumping to five conclusions based on a single round of matches.
Every week here on Opta Analyst, we do away with our usual approach of diving deep into the data and instead come to a load of conclusions based on a single round of Premier League fixtures.
Will any of our latest five knee-jerk reactions hold up in the weeks to come, or will they be disproven as the season goes on? Read on to see what you think.
There was a great deal of change at Chelsea over the summer but there have been plenty of indications in the early part of the Xabi Alonso era that his could be a productive reign.
But in Saturday’s dismal home defeat to Tottenham, this was Chelsea back to their self-destructive worst.

Yes, they were missing first-choice goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez and first-choice number nine João Pedro. And yes, Tottenham were very good and fully deserved the win. But this was a defeat in a game that Chelsea just do not lose – before this they had lost only once at home to rivals Spurs in the Premier League era.

Concerningly, though, losing has become too normalised for this club, and although it was a shock to see them beaten by Tottenham of all teams, the fans have had to grow used to seeing their team lose. In fact, since the start of March, Chelsea have lost 14 games – more than any other side not just in the Premier League, but in any of the top five European leagues.
14 – Since the start of March, Chelsea have lost more games in all competitions than any other side in Europe's big-five leagues (14).Stormy. pic.twitter.com/sOjWHQt0lo

Discipline remains a major issue, too, and several managers have been unable to resolve it. After Cole Palmer’s dismissal, Chelsea have picked up nine red cards since the start of last season, four more than anyone else. Morgan Rogers might have been sent off late on, too for a challenge on Conor Gallagher.
They have consistently had problems in goal, too, and on the evidence of his own goal here, Mike Penders could be yet another error-prone goalkeeper.
There are still big problems for Alonso to fix.

Last week, we can’t have been the only ones wondering what had happened to Arsenal’s set-piece threat. After breaking the Premier League record for goals from corners last season, they had gone seven games this season without scoring a single goal from a corner, or any kind of set-piece, for that matter.

That said, Arsenal had been more than making up for any issues with enough goals in open play, often scoring after long passages of possession with all of their players involved. They had won all but one of their games and looked far more convincing than last season, too.
But they were always going to run into some difficulties at some point, and Bukayo Saka’s injury is a hurdle they’ll have to navigate.

He is integral to their attacking play and Arsenal always look slightly less fluent without him. So it was no surprise that the display against Everton this weekend with Saka absent was a little more disjointed than some of their other performances this campaign.

But with Ezri Konsa’s seventh-minute opener, Arsenal proved they haven’t entirely lost their set-piece mojo. It was their first set-piece goal (excluding penalties) since May, ending a run of 13 games without one, and set them on their way to a win that felt like it belonged to last season, in that they broke the deadlock with a set-piece and then always looked like holding on.

They are a better team than last season, and set-pieces won’t be as necessary a route to goal, but winning through them is something they need to keep on doing, because they will have off days. If they do this many more times, they’ll stroll to the title.

The 10 teams involved in Sunday’s games completed just 75.8% of their passes. It was the lowest pass completion rate on a single day of Premier League football with at least five matches played since 14 December 2019, nearly seven years ago.

Some might assume the stormy conditions were the reason for so many passes going astray, and they might well be right. But there was also some really poor football on display, a lot of unconvincing performances and, most strikingly, almost everyone showed they have real weaknesses. That wasn’t limited to Sunday, either.
